stem: Why did the switch from iron rails to steel rails matter most for the railroad network?

stimulus.source_note: Nineteenth-century engraving of a Bessemer converter in operation, Wikimedia Commons. Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bessemer_process.jpg
stimulus.text: The image shows a Bessemer converter at work inside a steel mill. A large pear-shaped vessel throws off a shower of white-hot sparks as air blasts through molten iron. A ladle and tools lie in the foreground. The converter is the tall upright vessel in the center.

options.text: Steel rails were lighter, so trains could run without locomotives
options.misconception: Background: steel is heavier and stronger than iron, not lighter, and every train still needed a locomotive to pull it.

options.text: Steel rails let railroads charge farmers lower freight rates by law
options.misconception: Background: freight rates were set by the railroads and later regulated by government; the metal in the rails did not set rates by law.

options.text: Steel rails lasted far longer under heavy loads, so track stayed in service
Steel rails needed no maintenance, so railroads fired all their track crews
options.misconception: Background: steel rails still wore out and needed crews to inspect and replace them; they lasted longer, they did not last forever.

rationales.A: Background: steel rails were stronger than iron rails, not lighter. Trains still needed locomotives, and a lighter rail would have bent under heavy loads.
rationales.B: Background: railroads set their own freight rates, and farmers complained about them for decades. The metal in the rails did not change rates by law.
rationales.C: Background from the books: steel was far more durable than iron, so steel rails survived heavy trains that wore iron rails out quickly. Longer-lasting track let the network grow without constant rebuilding.
rationales.D: Background: steel rails wore out more slowly, but they still wore out. Railroads kept large track crews to inspect and replace rails.
rationales.general:
Ask what breaks first on a railroad: the rail.
1. Background: iron rails wore out fast under heavy trains, so track had to be rebuilt again and again.
2. Background: steel rails lasted far longer, so a line laid in steel stayed in service while the traffic over it grew.
3. Background: that durability is what let the network stretch to 190,000 miles without collapsing under its own weight.
Remember: a network grows when its weakest link stops breaking.
